title: The Call of Jeremiah
summary: The book opens by naming Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, and dating his ministry from King Josiah to the exile of Jerusalem. God tells Jeremiah that he knew and appointed him before he was born, overrules his protest that he is too young, and puts his words in his mouth. Two visions, an almond branch and a boiling pot tilting from the north, announce that God watches over his word and that disaster is coming, and God promises to make Jeremiah strong against all who oppose him.
story: Jeremiah's call comes late in the history of the kingdom of Judah. The northern kingdom of Israel had fallen to Assyria a century earlier, in 722 BC, and Judah had survived, sometimes faithful and often not. The prophets before Jeremiah, Isaiah among them, had warned that Judah too would be judged if it did not turn back. This chapter sets the stage for the last act: a young man is sent to tell the nation that the judgment is now close and that it will come from the north. Everything in the rest of the book grows from the six verbs of verse 10, to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant. Most of the book is spent on the first four; the last two are the hope that survives the ruin.
historical:
The heading dates Jeremiah's call to the thirteenth year of Josiah, about 627 BC, and runs his ministry to the fifth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year, the summer of 587 or 586 BC, when Jerusalem fell and its people were deported to Babylon. That span covers the whole collapse of Judah. Josiah (about 640 to 609 BC) was a reforming king who tore down idolatrous shrines, especially after a book of the law was found in the temple in 622 BC (2 Kings 22-23). After his death his sons Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah and his grandson Jehoiachin reigned in quick succession under pressure first from Egypt and then from Babylon. The heading names only the three kings whose reigns were long enough to matter, and the book itself goes on past 586 to events in Egypt.

Anathoth was a village of priests in the territory of Benjamin, a few miles northeast of Jerusalem. Solomon had banished the priest Abiathar there (1 Kings 2:26), and some scholars suggest that Jeremiah's family descended from that line, which would explain its distance from the Jerusalem temple establishment, though the text does not say so. Jeremiah's father Hilkiah is probably not the high priest Hilkiah who found the book of the law; the name was common.
cultural:
Jeremiah protests that he is only a child. The Hebrew word covers anyone from a baby to a young man not yet established, so he may have been a teenager or in his early twenties. In a culture that honored age, a young man had little standing to rebuke kings, priests, and elders. God's answer touches Jeremiah's mouth, echoing the way Isaiah's lips were touched with a coal (Isaiah 6:7) and fulfilling the promise of Deuteronomy 18:18 that God would raise up a prophet and put his words in his mouth.

The first vision depends on a pun. The almond was the first tree to blossom in Judah's late winter, and its Hebrew name, shaqed, sounds like the word for watching, shoqed; it was the waking tree. The second vision draws on the geography of the region. Armies from Mesopotamia did not cross the Arabian desert to reach Judah; they came around the Fertile Crescent and down from Syria in the north. A cooking pot on a fire, tilted and about to spill its boiling contents southward, pictured an invasion about to pour over the land.
literary: The chapter combines a superscription (verses 1 to 3) with a call narrative that follows a pattern seen in the calls of Moses (Exodus 3-4) and Gideon (Judges 6): God commissions, the one called objects, God reassures and gives a sign. Jeremiah's objection, I surely do not know how to speak, is close to Moses's own. The call is followed by two short visions, each introduced by the same question, what do you see, and each explained by wordplay or image. The chapter is framed by a repeated promise: I am with you to deliver you (verses 8 and 19). Verse 10 compresses the whole book's message into paired verbs, four of destruction and two of building, and these verbs reappear at key points later (for example 18:7-9 and 31:28).

outline.t: Heading: Jeremiah and the kings of his day
Known before birth and appointed a prophet
Vision of the almond branch: God watches his word
Vision of the boiling pot: disaster from the north
A fortified city: stand firm, I am with you

doctrines.note: The chapter shows how prophecy works: the word of the LORD comes to a person, God puts his words in the prophet's mouth, and the prophet must speak all that he is commanded. The prophet's message is God's word in human speech, and God watches over it to fulfill it.

God knew Jeremiah and set him apart before he was formed in the womb. His life was not an accident, and his calling was fitted to him before he could choose it. The same God directs the nations of the north as his instruments.

The coming invasion is God's judgment on Judah because the people have forsaken him and worshiped the works of their own hands. The disaster is not random history but a response to covenant unfaithfulness.

words.note: Yada, to know. In verse 5, God's knowing Jeremiah before birth is more than awareness; it carries the sense of choosing and committing oneself to someone, as in Amos 3:2 where God says he has known only Israel among the families of the earth. Jeremiah's reply in verse 6 uses the same verb: I do not know how to speak. God's knowing is set against Jeremiah's not knowing.

Shaqad, to watch or be wakeful. God's explanation of the almond vision (verse 12) plays on this verb and the almond's name, shaqed. God is awake over his word like a watchman, and it will not fail. The same verb returns in 31:28, where God promises that as he watched over them to uproot and tear down, he will watch over them to build and plant.

Natash, to uproot or pluck up, the first of the six verbs in verse 10. It pictures a gardener pulling out a plant by its roots. Paired with to plant at the end of the list, it frames Jeremiah's ministry as the work of a gardener who must clear before he can sow.

Tsaphon, north. In Jeremiah the north is the direction of danger: the foe from the north appears again and again in chapters 4 to 6 before it is finally identified with Babylon (25:9). For the first hearers the enemy was not yet named, which made the threat more unsettling.

christ: Jeremiah's call, like Moses's, shapes the Bible's picture of the true prophet who speaks God's words, and the New Testament presents Jesus as that prophet in the fullest sense (Acts 3:22-23 applies Deuteronomy 18 to him). Where Jeremiah received God's words, Jesus is himself the Word made flesh (John 1:14). Paul echoes Jeremiah's call when he says God set him apart before he was born and called him by his grace to preach among the nations (Galatians 1:15-16); like Jeremiah, Paul was a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah's commission to uproot and to plant also prepares for the gospel's pattern: judgment on sin is real, but God's final purpose is to build and plant, a purpose Christians see accomplished in the new covenant Jeremiah will announce in chapter 31.

hard.q: Does verse 5 mean that God plans everything about every person's life before birth?
hard.a:
Verse 5 is often quoted in two debates: about God's sovereignty and human freedom, and about the value of unborn life. In context it is a specific word to Jeremiah about his calling as a prophet, not a general statement about every person's destiny. God knew him, set him apart, and appointed him before he was born, which tells us that his vocation came from God's initiative, not his own. Theologians in the Reformed tradition see here an instance of God's sovereign election of individuals for his purposes; those in other traditions emphasize that Jeremiah still had to respond, protested, and later struggled bitterly with his calling.

Many Christians also cite the verse, alongside Psalm 139:13-16, as evidence that God's relationship with a person begins before birth. That use draws a broader principle from a verse whose main subject is prophetic calling, but it rests on a real feature of the text: God speaks of knowing Jeremiah in the womb as a person, not merely as a possibility.

questions: Jeremiah objected that he was too young and did not know how to speak. What objections do you raise when you sense God asking something of you?
God's promise was not that Jeremiah would be spared opposition but that he would not be overcome. How is that different from the kind of promise we usually want?
The six verbs of verse 10 include both tearing down and building. Where might God need to uproot something before he plants something new?
